source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: First direct test of RPD-style prompting on LLMs. Two prompts based on NDM (recognition-primed and data-frame) beat a plain prompt on care-seeking triage across 10 ChatGPT models.
numbers: 45 real patient vignettes x 3 urgency levels (2 emergency, 30 nonemergency, 13 self-care by implication) x 10 models x 3 prompts x 10 repeats. Mean accuracy: default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7), recognition-primed 67.6% (66.3-69), data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68). Mixed logistic regression: RP OR 2.26 (z=8.69), DF OR 2.05 (z=7.23), both p<.001.
limits: One domain (self-triage), one vendor family. Gain is 4.3 points absolute. Prompt may help partly by adding reasoning to non-reasoning models. Not a test of the real RPD mechanism, only of a prompt that names it.
agent_relevance: A recognition-style instruction (match case to a known pattern, then check it) can add a few points on ill-defined judgment tasks. Small effect; test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: The gain is concentrated in the hardest class, self-care cases, where plain models almost never gave the low-urgency answer. Emergency and nonemergency accuracy did not drop.
numbers: Self-care accuracy: default 13.4% -> RP 29.8% -> DF 24.6%. GPT-4.1 self-care 0% -> 43.8% (RP) and 39.2% (DF). GPT-4o self-care 2.3% -> 16.2% (RP). o4 mini (already gave some self-care): 46.9% -> 63.8% (RP), 56.2% (DF). Emergency n=2 stayed 100% for most models; GPT-4.1 DF fell to 80%.
limits: Only 2 emergency cases, so no safety conclusion. Effect looks like removing a default over-triage bias, not better recognition.
agent_relevance: Recognition framing may work by unlocking the base-rate-favored 'nothing serious' answer. Useful against a model's habitual over-escalation.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Effect is not uniform. Reasoning models gained more than non-reasoning ones, and the newest family (GPT-5.2) did not gain at all.
numbers: Interaction vs non-reasoning: RP OR 2.15 (z=4.05, p<.001), DF OR 1.70 (z=2.65, p=.008). Largest single gain: GPT-4.1 mini 49.8% -> 62.4% with DF (+13 points, CI 9.7-16.1). GPT-5.2 Instant 57.8 / 56.4 / 55.3 and GPT-5.2 Thinking 52.0 / 53.1 / 51.8 (default / RP / DF). o4 mini high 68.9 / 71.3 / 70.7. Same result at low temperature and for binary care vs self-care.
quote: Both NDM-inspired prompts increased overall model accuracy
limits: Authors say effects held 'across all tested models except GPT-5.2'. Output variability was similar across prompts.
agent_relevance: Benefit shrinks or vanishes on strongest models. The scaffold must prove itself per model (G7); do not assume transfer.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Study 1: elite chess players blunder more under blitz than standard time control. If expertise were mostly recognition, time pressure should matter little. It matters a lot.
numbers: 20 grandmasters, within-subject, standard vs blitz tournaments. Proportion of blunders 0.20 [0.18,0.22] -> 0.27 [0.24,0.29], t(19)=6.54, d=1.39. Mean blunder size 0.98 -> 1.45 pawns, t(19)=4.23, d=0.96. Expected blunder per move 0.20 -> 0.38, t(19)=5.79, d=1.30; worse for 18 of 20 players. EBPM validated vs outcomes: winners 0.15 vs losers 0.39 (standard).
limits: Archival chess data; chess moves are not fireground decisions. Blitz is also a harsher time limit than fire commanders face. Blunder measure from Fritz engine.
agent_relevance: Recognition alone does not carry expert quality when time is cut. Supports a design where quick mode is allowed but a slower check can be bought when stakes or novelty are high.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Study 2: 7 world champions' time-per-move shows experts spend time selectively. They move fast when it is safe and slow on hard moves. Fast moves made under time pressure carry more blunders and some huge ones.
numbers: Study 2 sample: 7 world chess champions, archival, different time controls. Authors report blunder propensity rises as play is forced to rely on fast moves; some fast moves are accurate, others become big blunders (their Figs 2-4).
quote: experts ... intuit when feasible and to deliberate when necessary
limits: Exact Study 2 coefficients were not extracted in this read; only the summary statements.
agent_relevance: The skill is the switch, not the recognition itself. Matches S0 quick mode plus an escalation signal (G1: doubt only on a signal).

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: Review of the chess-speed literature that was used to support recognition-based expertise, with the main challenges to it.
numbers: Gobet & Simon (1996, 2000): Kasparov slightly weaker in simultaneous play; Montero (2019) and Van Harreveld et al. (2007): his Elo fell from 2750 to 2646, about 60th place in the world. Chabris & Hearst (2003): grandmasters (Elo 2530-2790) made more and larger blunders in 15-minute rapid games. Chang & Lane (2016): even in blitz, stronger players (Elo 2300-2397) took long on selected moves. Burns (2004) 3 class B vs 3 masters in blitz; masters looked immune but the quality measure was weak.
limits: Second-hand summary of other papers; those papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: The 'experts are immune to time pressure' evidence is weak. Do not rely on it to justify skipping checks.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cogn Res Princ Implic)
finding: The authors argue the RPD model puts the weight on intuition and quote Klein's own claim that experienced people rarely choose among several options. They propose that training must also build deliberation for novel cases (Sully example).
numbers: Cites Cohen-Hatton & Honey (2015): goal-oriented training changed fire and rescue commanders to formulate plans before acting, without slowing response to unexpected events.
quote: people with experience rarely engage in the process of choosing among several options
limits: Opinion paper on top of archival data. Klein's model does include mental simulation (variation 3), which the authors acknowledge.
agent_relevance: A concrete training result that deliberation can be added to recognition-driven commanders without latency cost. Supports a cheap 'state goal and expected outcome before acting' step.

source: Assessing military professionals' endorsement of decision-making assumptions: exploratory factor analysis (2026)
finding: Survey of how military professionals endorse Klein's 11 claims (procedures, biases, logic over intuition, options, more information, early conclusions). Endorsement splits in two factors, not one.
numbers: N=225 Norwegian Armed Forces personnel (2024-2025). 9 of 11 items kept. KMO 0.741; Bartlett chi2(36)=282.86, p<.001. Two factors explain 29.24% of variance: Planning/Structure and Analytic/Evidence-based. Alpha 0.65 and about 0.71.
limits: Attitude survey, not behavior. Low variance explained. Klein's claims were not built as test items. Authors note few NDM studies use psychometric methods (citing Reale et al. 2023).
agent_relevance: Even trained practitioners do not hold one coherent view of recognition versus analysis. Treat the dichotomy as two tools.

source: Cognitive task analysis to evaluate resident physician decision making in the ICU (2025)
finding: Critical Decision Method interviews coded with the RPD model as template, on septic-shock fluid decisions. Residents relied on intuition and volume heuristics more than on measured predictors, and showed biases.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible third-year residents interviewed (median 7 days after the event, IQR 6.5-11). Seven domains: cues, information, decision making, alternatives, analogs, expected outcomes, goals. Heuristic: patients given more than 3-5 L assumed not to benefit from more fluid. Found premature closure, confirmation bias, status quo bias.
limits: Small, single center, self-selected, retrospective recall.
agent_relevance: Where recognition rests on thin experience it gives heuristics that ignore evidence. A fast match is only as good as the pattern store behind it.

source: Le Menn, Bossard, Travassos, Duarte (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study (J Hum Kinet)
finding: RPD coding of an expert handball goalkeeper's video-cued recall. Most saves were simple pattern matches; a third needed mental simulation; a fifth needed diagnosis.
numbers: 26 shot sequences, 83 accounts of decisions, 419 units of meaning. Simple match 38 (46%), simulation 28 (34%), diagnosis 17 (20%). Units: cues 44%, expectancies 22%, actions 18%, knowledge 10%, plausible goals 4%, consequences 2%.
limits: One goalkeeper. Self-report after the fact. The coding scheme brings its own categories; no emotion.
agent_relevance: All three RPD paths are used by one expert in one task. A mix, not a single mode.

source: Le Menn, Bossard, Travassos, Duarte (2019) Handball goalkeeper intuitive decision-making: a naturalistic case study (J Hum Kinet)
finding: Distance to the thrower (less time) changes the micro-decision but not the type of recognition process.
numbers: Mean distance: simple match 7.17 +/- 3.13 m; simulation 7.81 +/- 6.06 m; diagnosis 9.15 +/- 6.94 m. Non-parametric tests: distance affected micro-decision categories, not recognition process types.
limits: Large SDs, overlapping ranges; one participant.
agent_relevance: Weak support for more time meaning more diagnosis. Time budget should be a soft input to path choice.

source: Naturalistic decision-making in sport: how current advances in the RPD model offer insights (Front Psychol, 2022)
finding: Review of RPD tests in sport, with proportions of the three paths.
numbers: Macquet (2020) as cited: 60-81% of expert decisions simple matching, 13-28% diagnosis, 3-24% evaluating a course of action. Earlier sport option-generation work: experts chose their preferred first option in about 80% of decisions.
limits: Second-hand via this review (Macquet 2020 not opened). Coding varies across studies.
agent_relevance: A base rate for the S0 default: roughly 3 in 4 decisions are first-match in sport. The real task mix for an agent must be measured, not borrowed.

source: Naturalistic decision-making in sport: how current advances in the RPD model offer insights (Front Psychol, 2022)
finding: Boundary conditions and individual differences in sport RPD research.
numbers: Collins et al. (2016): rugby coaches, with less time pressure than players, made more deliberate decisions. Kermarrec & Bossard (2014), Le Menn et al. (2019): players far from the ball had time for simulation and diagnosis. Klatt et al. (2019): creativity scores correlated positively with first-option quality (no coefficient given). Roca et al. (2018): most creative soccer players had broader attention, more and shorter fixations. Baylor (2001): proposed U-shaped intuition development.
limits: Mostly correlational; no coefficients. The review says there is little consistent evidence for an intuitive-analytic continuum in sport.
agent_relevance: Time slack predicts the analytic share. First-option quality depends on the pattern store.

source: Hinz et al. (2022) Differences in decision-making behavior between elite and amateur team-handball players in a near-game test (Front Psychol)
finding: Elite and amateur handball players differ in what they choose, not clearly in how fast. Authors discuss take-the-first and later corrective switches (dynamic inconsistency).
numbers: 44 male players (22 elite, mean age 17.59; 22 amateurs, 20.71). Left-handed breakthrough: elite chose forward/tackling more, chi2(14)=25.06, p=.033, OR 2.76 (1.54-4.95). Pass: OR 3.00 (1.78-5.04); amateurs chose passive/blocking, OR 2.70. Decision time fell with more visual information; expertise main effect not significant. Travassos et al. (2013) meta-analysis: no expertise effect on decision time in situ, p=0.82 (2 studies).
limits: Video occlusion test, not live play. The paper does not report percent of first options chosen and does not mention RPD.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is in choice quality, not speed. Do not measure quick mode by latency alone.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox (Front Psychol)
finding: History of NDM and the headline RPD claim, plus the replication list Klein and Wright give.
numbers: 1989 workshop with about 30 researchers; book Decision making in action (Klein et al. 1993). RPD 'accounted for 80-90% of the decisions that firefighters made'. Replications named: military leaders (Schmitt & Klein 1999), firefighters (Keren et al. 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998). Tested with support: Klein et al. (1995), Johnson & Raab (2003). Argument: RPD needs 10-20 years of experience, so student labs cannot find it.
limits: Written by the model's founder; replications are listed, not described, and not independent. The 80-90% wording differs from the primary report's under-12% comparison figure (see a24).
agent_relevance: RPD is a claim about experienced people in familiar fields. An LLM has no 10-20 years of tracked outcome feedback, only text patterns.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox (Front Psychol)
finding: NDM widened into macrocognition (planning, sensemaking, uncertainty management, expertise development) and then into training tools such as ShadowBox.
numbers: Stages: NDM (1980s to 1989), macrocognitive models (Klein et al. 2003; Klein et al. 2000 defined macro vs micro cognition), then methods and tools. The Vincennes shootdown a year before 1989 pushed the Navy TADMUS program.
limits: Narrative history, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Links to the sensemaking and data-frame subfields; hand off there.

source: Thanasuan & Mueller (2014) Crossword expertise as recognitional decision making: an AI approach (Front Psychol)
finding: Computational model of crossword solving built on a Bayesian recognitional-decision retrieval mechanism, compared with experts and novices. Retrieve a best candidate, check constraints, little backtracking.
numbers: Only Models 1 and 5 (fast retrieval, high recovery) finished with expert-like timing and accuracy; they beat all novices but did not quite reach experts. Slow, disfluent models (4, 8) did worse than most novices. Fluent models solved 70-90% of clues given time. Models 3 and 7 plateaued near 75% completion.
limits: Closed-form task. A retrieval model, not a full RPD model (no mental simulation).
agent_relevance: A working template of a recognition solver. Experts rarely backtrack, so first-pass quality dominates.

source: Thanasuan & Mueller (2014) Crossword expertise as recognitional decision making: an AI approach (Front Psychol)
finding: Human crossword data: experts finish fast and almost error free; novices do not finish. Experts solve clues with partial letters filled in, which strengthens the match.
numbers: Experts: all finished in 5.3 +/- 2.5 min, 77.2 of 78 correct (SD 1.5). Novices: none finished in 25 min; 23.9 +/- 9.4 complete, 23.1 +/- 9.5 correct. Experts reach about 40% pre-filled letters after the first few clues; novices only near the end.
limits: Small sample; one puzzle.
agent_relevance: Experts order problems so cues are stronger. An agent can reorder subgoals to maximise cues before it commits.

source: Thanasuan & Mueller (2014) Crossword expertise as recognitional decision making: an AI approach (Front Psychol)
finding: Orthographic cues are a second, cheaper recognition route that experts use better than novices.
numbers: Cited prior work (Mueller & Thanasuan 2013): with 3 or fewer missing letters experts guess above 80% even on hard clues; novices 40-50%.
limits: Cited secondhand from the 2014 paper.
agent_relevance: Partial structural cues raise match accuracy a lot. Build constraint hints from neighbouring parts into S0.

source: Wikipedia: Recognition primed decision
finding: Plain statement of the three RPD variations and the first-adequate-option rule.
numbers: V1: situation and response known (if..then). V2: response known, situation needs diagnosis. V3: situation known, response unknown; simulate until one fits. Source is Klein (1998) pp. 1-30. No study numbers.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, tagged as needing citations. States limits: needs extensive experience; misrecognition in unusual cases.
agent_relevance: The three variations map to three S0 branches: answer, diagnose, simulate.

source: Gary Klein site: RPD page
finding: Klein's own statement: RPD was developed in 1985 by Klein, Calderwood and Clinton-Cirocco; experienced commanders pick and carry out an action without generating and comparing a set of options.
numbers: Only number on the page is the year 1985.
quote: people can use experience to generate a plausible option as the first one they consider
limits: Promotional page, no data.
agent_relevance: The claim to test is that the first option is plausible and often adequate, not that it is optimal.

source: Instructional-design blog: The Recognition-Primed Decision Model (idtips substack), secondary summary
finding: Secondary summary of the fireground study numbers, attributed to the 2010 reprint.
numbers: 26 experienced commanders, mean 23 years of service; 156 decision points; over 80% with no option comparison; under 12% with side-by-side comparison. Simple match said to take 8-16 s (unsourced). Mental simulation typically about 3 variables and 6 transitions (Klein 1998).
limits: Blog-level source. About 8% of decisions unaccounted for. The 8-16 s figure is unsourced.
agent_relevance: Working memory caps simulation at a few variables and steps. Cap the simulate branch to that size.

source: Instructional-design blog: The Recognition-Primed Decision Model (idtips substack), secondary summary
finding: Training evidence tied to Klein's methods, with sample sizes and gains.
numbers: Chase & Simon (1973): masters recall positions after 5 s but no better than novices on random layouts. ShadowBox (Klein, Hintze & Saab 2013): Marines n=59, 3 h, 28% better alignment with experts than control; Fort Benning 1 h tablet, 21%. Facilitation adds about 6% (Klein & Borders 2016), not significant. CTA-based training meta-analysis (Tofel-Grehl & Feldon 2013): Hedges g=0.871.
limits: All second-hand; originals not opened. 'Alignment with experts' is a self-defined measure.
agent_relevance: Expert-alignment scoring (rank cues, compare to a held-out expert key) is a cheap check for an agent.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1985/1986/2010) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (ARI TR 796; HFS Proc.; JCEDM 4(3):186-209)
finding: Founding study. The report could not be downloaded (HTTP 403). Facts here come from a web-search summary of the report, not from reading it.
numbers: 156 decision points probed by interview; fewer than 12% showed simultaneous comparison of two or more options (search summary). Secondary sources disagree: 80%, 80-90%, 81.4%, and '117 of 134 decisions' appear online. None checked against the report.
limits: Not opened. Counts conflict. Interview recall, not observation.
agent_relevance: Use 80-90% recognition only as an approximate claim until the report is read.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (2010) The original study plus a postscript, JCEDM
finding: Reprint of the 1985 study with new commentary by Klein. Could not be opened. Listed as the home of the numbers.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Next step: obtain the postscript for Klein's own account of what the study could not show.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (Am Psychol 64(6):515-526)
finding: Joint paper of a heuristics-and-biases and an NDM researcher. Boundary: intuitive judgment is trustworthy only if the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the person has had a chance to learn it, with quick feedback.
numbers: Europe PMC citation count 389. No study numbers verified.
quote: two conditions: an environment that is sufficiently regular to be predictable, and an opportunity to learn these regularities
limits: Full text not opened (login page and blocked copies). Content from search summaries.
agent_relevance: Key boundary for S0: use the quick path only where outcome feedback was available. A language model's practice has no tracked outcomes in most domains.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first (Organ Behav Hum Decis Process 91(2):215-229); Raab & Johnson (2007) Expertise-based differences in search and option-generation
finding: Handball experiments testing take-the-first. Search summary of the 2007 abstract: the first option generated was generally better than later ones, few options were generated, and no expertise difference in choosing the initial option.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened; search summary only.
agent_relevance: This is the empirical core of 'first option usually good'. Check original numbers before use.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Authors' own limits: LLM prompting mostly targets well-structured, low-uncertainty tasks; NDM prompts help in ill-defined tasks and are untested on well-defined ones.
numbers: Single benchmark, 45 vignettes, 2 emergency cases; each combination run 10 times. Benefit 'thus far limited to uncertain tasks'.
limits: No replication yet. No chain-of-thought-only baseline in the parts read.
agent_relevance: A fair test for our agent: ill-defined versus well-defined tasks, recognition prompt versus plain chain-of-thought at equal tokens.
